title: Can Empirical Catch Allocation Strategies Based on Single‐Region Stock Assessments Provide Adequate Advice for Managing Spatially Structured Fish Populations?
content:
ABSTRACT

Spatial structure and movement are common features of marine fish populations, yet many fisheries management systems continue to rely on single-region stock assessments. When stock-level catch advice is generated at a broader spatial scale than management implementation, empirical catch allocation strategies provide a way to distribute harvest among regions and fleets. However, the performance of spatial catch allocation approaches remains poorly understood in terms of their ability to achieve robust management outcomes, especially when confronted with uncertainty in underlying population structure, movement and recruitment dynamics. Using a closed-loop management strategy evaluation (MSE) conditioned on a demersal fish population (western Atlantic black sea bass, Centropristis striata), we compared uniform, catch-based, survey-based, and catch-survey hybrid catch allocation strategies across operating model scenarios that varied in population structure, movement directionality and magnitude, and recruitment dynamics. Across scenarios, catch allocation strategy generally affected regional outcomes more strongly than system-level outcomes, redistributing catch, biomass, interannual variability in catch and depletion risk among regions. Differences among strategies were modest under bidirectional movement and recruitment varying around regional means, but stronger regional tradeoffs emerged when movement was unidirectional or recruitment declined in one population component. Uniform and catch-based strategies generally produced steadier catches, whereas survey-based strategies were more responsive to changes in regional biomass distribution but increased interannual variability in catch. No single strategy consistently outperformed others across metrics or spatial scales. Empirical catch allocation can provide a useful bridge between spatially aggregated assessment advice and spatial management, but its performance is conditional on underlying spatial processes.
